name: Sara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm Sara, I'm 27, and I'm head shepherd at High Cross, a hill farm run by a land trust. We've got about 1,100 ewes on the open hill, a few suckler cows and some hay meadows down by the river. I've got one other shepherd, Dan, and extra hands at lambing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In spring it's lambing, so I'm up at four checking the sheds and out on the quad bike by six. The rest of the year it's gathering the hill with the dogs, which can take a whole day for one block of ground. Then there's scanning, shearing, foot trimming, and making hay in July if we get four dry days together. I love being up on the tops on a clear morning with the dogs working well. What wears me out is the sheer distance, and losing ewes in a bad snow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in the farm cottage with Nell, my best dog. My mum is in the village and I eat with her on Sundays. I use AI now and then, mostly to check a dose for a wormer or ask about a sick ewe before I ring the vet. We started using virtual fencing collars last year, but only after the farm over the valley had them working for two seasons. I've got about three months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine with that. The hill doesn't care about hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be like this up here. AI can help with the record-keeping and the vet forms, but it can't gather 400 ewes off a wet hill in a mist. That's a dog and a person who knows the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. There are things I'd like help with, like spotting a lame ewe from a drone before she's been lame a week. But mostly I'd be glad the trust doesn't start asking whether they need two shepherds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd use the AI for paperwork a bit more, because I hate the movement records, and maybe trial a camera in the lambing shed if somebody else proves it works first. I'd keep putting a bit by each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry gather with every sheep in the pen by lunchtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the time saved to go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper days off, honestly. I haven't had a full weekend in March or April since I was 21. If the paperwork took half the time, I could go to my cousin's wedding without feeling guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the village change in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, and that's the trouble. Young people would still leave because there's no housing and no work. AI wouldn't fix that, and it wouldn't make it worse either.

S0.say: I'd say AI can help with record-keeping and vet forms, but it can't gather 400 ewes off a wet hill in a mist. That still needs a dog and a person who knows the ground.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved and a little disappointed. I'd like help spotting a lame ewe earlier, but mostly I'd be glad the trust doesn't start asking whether it needs two shepherds.
S0.do: Keeps going as now and uses AI more for movement records and paperwork. Trials a camera in the lambing shed only if another farm proves it first, and keeps saving a little each month.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, with a small wish that the tools did a bit more.
S0.quote: AI can help with the record-keeping and the vet forms, but it can't gather 400 ewes off a wet hill in a mist.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is practical and grounded, and the plateau barely touches her. What stood out was that her biggest wish isn't more output but proper days off. She sees the village's problems, housing and young people leaving, as having nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's more what I expect, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change is fine as long as the benefits stay on the hill. If drones and collars save the trust money, put it into shepherds' wages and houses for young families in the village. I'd say that to the trust board and I'd put it on the farmers' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be okay but Dan wouldn't. Drones that count sheep and collars that move them could do half his job. I'm the one who makes the decisions, he's the one who does the legwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the first farm in the valley go fully onto drones and collars, then I'd ask the trust to send me on a course. In the first year I'd probably learn to fly a drone for gathering, because it's proven in some places already. I'd also push the trust to keep Dan on and train him too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Dan, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, over a cup of tea in the lambing shed, because he deserves that. I'd say learn the drone with me, and if the trust won't pay for both of us, I'll make a fuss. He's 45 and he's got two kids at the high school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides how the savings get shared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust board, and most of them live in the city. They mean well, but they think about birds and peat bogs more than people. That's why I'd want a shepherds' association with some real say.

S1.say: I'd say the change is fine as long as the savings stay on the hill, in shepherds' wages and houses for young families. I'd say it to the trust board and on the farmers' group chat.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd be okay, because I make the decisions, but Dan wouldn't. Drones and collars could do half of his legwork.
S1.do: Waits for the first valley farm to go fully onto drones, then asks the trust for training and learns to fly a gathering drone in the first year. Pushes the trust to keep and retrain her colleague Dan, and backs a shepherds' association.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of her colleague rather than herself.
S1.quote: I'm the one who makes the decisions, he's the one who does the legwork.
S1.fieldNote: Sara's steady streak shows clearly: she waits for proof next door, then moves. Her worry is for Dan, a 45-year-old with children, more than for herself. She blames distant trust board members who think about birds and bogs more than people, and wants a collective voice for shepherds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's two lambings. I don't think anybody's ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when the government has to protect people in places like ours. Hill farming already runs on public support, so it should be easy to keep people on the land as caretakers, even if robots do the shepherding. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trust would replace both of us before the hay was in. They're a charity, they'd have to. And hill sheep don't make money, so I'm not even sure anybody would keep sheep up here at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, like the new quad bike I've been saving for. I'd join the farmers' union lobbying and go to the regional capital for the protest. And I'd ask the trust whether there's a job looking after the land itself, the walls, the peat, the paths, if the sheep go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sick in my stomach, but I'd still be thinking straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Nell in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stay with me, wherever I went. That's the stupid thing that got me, actually, thinking about a robot gathering the hill and my dog lying by the stove with nothing to do. She'd hate it more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two years be enough time for you to change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Two years is long enough to panic and not long enough to train. Three months of savings covers one bad winter, not a new career.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to protect people in places like ours, and keep people on the land as caretakers even if robots do the shepherding. I'd be loud about it.
S2.think: Privately I think the trust would replace both shepherds before the hay was in. Hill sheep don't pay, so maybe nobody would keep them at all.
S2.do: Shelves the new quad bike and other big spending. Joins farmers' union lobbying and a protest in the regional capital, and asks the trust about a land-care job looking after walls, peat and paths.
S2.feel: Anxious and sick to her stomach, but still thinking clearly.
S2.quote: Two years is long enough to panic and not long enough to train.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Sara swings to politics and to looking for a caretaker role on the same land. The image that moved her most was her dog lying idle by the stove. She knows her three months of savings would cover a bad winter, not a career change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to do something, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get this right for hill communities, so let's not waste it. Housing, land-care jobs and a fair share of whatever the robots earn. I'd start a proper campaign, with the other shepherds in the valley, not just moan online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I could get ahead of it. I'm good with people and I know the hill better than anyone. If I learned the machines early, I'd be the one the trust kept to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a course on drones and land management, and I'd ask the trust to pay half. I'd start meeting with the other shepherds once a month about setting up a co-operative to share machines. I'd try to get my savings from three months to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. That makes all the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the slower picture you'd wait for others to go first. Would you still wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year, not more. With five years, waiting to see is a luxury, and I'm not daft. I'd let the farm over the valley try it first, then I'd be second, not tenth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-operative actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Own the drones and the robots between us, so the money stays in the valley. Hire out a team to look after the hill. It's what our grandparents did with the shearing gang, just with machines.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to get this right for hill communities, with housing, land-care jobs and a fair share of what robots earn. I'd start a real campaign with the other valley shepherds.
S3.think: Privately I think I could get ahead of it. If I learned the machines early, I'd be the one the trust kept to run them.
S3.do: Takes a course on drones and land management in year one, half paid by the trust. Meets monthly with valley shepherds to set up a co-operative that owns machines together, and builds savings from three to six months.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier, because she has a plan.
S3.quote: It's what our grandparents did with the shearing gang, just with machines.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough to turn Sara from worried to organised. She cut her usual wait-and-see from 'let others go first' to 'second, not tenth'. Her co-operative idea draws on an old shared-labour tradition, which gives her progressive views a local root.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That feels like a long way off, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. I'd want the government to fund training now, not in year nine. I'd say that on the radio if anyone asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a good run first. Ten more lambings, maybe the best years of my working life. After that I'd want to be part of whatever comes next on this hill, not watching from the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd carry on, save a bit, and learn the new kit as the valley takes it up. Around year five I'd help set up the co-operative and maybe do a part-time course in land management. I'd also think about putting my name down for one of the trust's houses, because I'd want to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like knowing winter's coming in October, not in the middle of a lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you think about your own future, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. With two years I'd freeze. With ten, I'd probably think about a partner and maybe kids, and I'd want them to grow up here. I'd just want to know there'd be a school still open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my habit, waiting for proof. I'd have to set myself a date, like I do for weaning lambs. If I hadn't started a course by 32, I'd know I'd let it slip.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so nobody should be left behind. The government should fund training now, not in year nine.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd get my best working years first, ten more lambings. After that I'd want to be part of what comes next on this hill, not watching from the village.
S4.do: Carries on and saves for the first few years while learning new kit as the valley adopts it. Helps set up a shepherds' co-operative around year five, starts a part-time land management course by 32, and applies for a trust house to stay local.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a quiet worry about leaving things too late.
S4.quote: Ten more lambings, maybe the best years of my working life.
S4.fieldNote: For Sara, ten years means she can plan her life, not just her job: a partner, children, and a village school she wants kept open. She knows her habit of waiting for proof and sets herself a deadline to beat it. Her vision of the future is still rooted in one place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's long enough to panic and not long enough to train, I said that and I meant it. What would help is land-care jobs funded properly, so people like me and Dan can stay on the hill looking after it, even if the sheep are gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the village. If the farms go, the school goes, the shop goes, and then it's just holiday cottages. That's what keeps me awake more than the robots.

headlineQuote: Ten more lambings, maybe the best years of my working life.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old head shepherd on a hill farm owned by a land trust, living alone with her dog Nell and close to her mum in the village. She's progressive, wants the savings from new machines kept in hill communities, and distrusts a city-based board deciding for the valley. She waits for proof before trying new tools, but with more warning she shortens that wait and moves to organise a co-operative. The fast scenario frightens her mainly for her colleague Dan and the village; the ten-year one lets her picture a full life there.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is long enough to panic but not long enough to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Properly funded land-care jobs so shepherds can stay on the hill looking after it, and a strong voice for the village so the school and shop survive.
